Designing software that survives its second year

EngineeringBy the OneClicq team9 November 20266 min read

Launch day gets the attention, but the real test of business software comes in year two. That is when new requirements arrive, the original developers have moved on, and every change seems to break something else.

Why software ages badly

Software rarely fails all at once. It slows down: features take longer, bugs return, and the team becomes afraid to touch certain parts. The causes are predictable, and so are the habits that prevent them.

1. Draw clear boundaries early

Group code by business area, such as orders, billing, inventory and users, rather than by technical layer. Each area should own its data and expose a small, well-defined interface to the rest of the system. When the billing rules change, you then change one area, not twenty files across the codebase.

You do not need microservices to do this. A well-organised single application, often called a modular monolith, is cheaper to run and easier to change for most businesses.

2. Keep business rules out of the screens

Discount rules, approval limits and tax calculations hidden in buttons and forms get copied, and the copies drift apart. Put them in one place in the backend, test them there, and let every screen, API and report call the same logic.

3. Test what would hurt

Aim for useful tests rather than a coverage percentage. Automated tests should protect the paths that cost money or trust when they break: payments, invoicing, permissions, data imports and key calculations. Run them on every change so problems are caught in minutes, not by customers.

4. Automate the boring operations

  • One-command deployments through a CI/CD pipeline, so releasing is routine rather than an event.
  • Database migrations in code, versioned alongside the application.
  • Monitoring and alerts for errors, slow pages and failed jobs, so you hear about problems before users do.
  • Automatic backups that are restored and tested regularly, not just taken.

5. Write down the decisions, not just the code

New developers can read code; what they cannot see is why it was written that way. Keep short decision records: what was decided, the options considered and why. Add a setup guide that gets someone running locally in under an hour. This is what lets a business change teams without losing momentum.

6. Plan for upgrades from the start

Frameworks, libraries and operating systems all reach end of support. Budget a little time every month to keep dependencies current, rather than facing a risky, expensive upgrade every few years. It is also one of the simplest security measures available.

7. Measure how it is really used

Usage data shows which features matter and which nobody touches. Removing unused features is one of the cheapest ways to make a system simpler to maintain.

A quick year-two health check

  • Can a new developer set up the project and make a small change in their first day?
  • Can you deploy safely on a weekday afternoon?
  • Do automated tests cover payments, permissions and key calculations?
  • Are all major dependencies still supported by their vendors?
  • Would you know within minutes if a key process failed overnight?

If the answer to any of these is no, that is where to invest next.
